Your application is written in which lan: Answer with the actual stack and be specific about the mix if it's polyglot (e.g. 'Python for the API layer, a Node.js frontend, some legacy Java services') - naming the real languages and roughly how much of your work touches each sets accurate expectations for any follow-up language-specific questions.
Have you deployed Sentinel antivirus? Is: Answer with actual scope - Sentinel/EDR agents for Kubernetes are typically deployed as a DaemonSet giving node-level and container-runtime visibility (scanning running container processes and node-level activity), distinct from scanning container images at build/registry time, which is a separate concern usually handled by a different tool (Trivy, Prisma Cloud image scanning).
How do you integrate Sentinel with your: Sentinel is deployed as a DaemonSet so it runs on every node, monitoring runtime behavior (process activity, file system changes, network connections) of containers as they execute - this is distinct from image scanning, which happens earlier, at CI/CD build time or in the registry, before the image is ever deployed. The two together cover both pre-deployment (image vulnerabilities) and runtime (active threat detection) security.
After deployment, how do you monitor the: Prisma Cloud (or a similar CSPM tool) continuously scans the cloud environment's configuration against security best-practice policies - flagging overly broad IAM grants (a service account with Owner instead of a scoped role), publicly exposed storage buckets or database instances, missing encryption, and open security groups/firewall rules - surfacing these as prioritized findings so the team can remediate before they're exploited, rather than relying on periodic manual audits.
You mentioned PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Mon: Answer honestly about the actual depth - most DevOps/platform roles handle operational database tasks (backups, monitoring, basic tuning, provisioning via Terraform) without being a full DBA (deep schema design, replication topology design, license management) - clarifying this distinction sets accurate expectations for follow-up depth.
What database-related activities have yo: List the specific activities you've actually done with concrete examples - e.g. 'set up automated backup schedules and tested restore procedures, provisioned Cloud SQL instances via Terraform, managed IAM database roles' - rather than a generic 'yes to all of the above' answer.
How do you take a backup of a PostgreSQL: `pg_dump <database> > backup.sql` for a logical backup of a single database (or `pg_dumpall` for the whole cluster including roles), or `pg_basebackup` for a physical base backup used for point-in-time recovery setups. Managed services like Cloud SQL handle this automatically via configured automated backup schedules plus point-in-time recovery using transaction logs, which is the standard approach for production rather than manual pg_dump scripting.
How do you restore a PostgreSQL backup?: For a logical dump, `psql <database> < backup.sql` (or `pg_restore` for a custom-format dump) replays the SQL to recreate the database's data. For point-in-time recovery from a managed service, restoring is typically a console/CLI operation selecting a target timestamp, which the service reconstructs from the base backup plus replayed transaction logs up to that point.
Have you performed backup and restore ac: Answer honestly - whether you've configured automated backup policies (common) versus actually executed and validated a full restore (less commonly tested until it's actually needed) - and if you have tested a restore, mention it specifically, since an untested backup strategy is a common and risky gap worth being honest about either way.
What database migration have you done, f: If you have direct experience, describe the source/target, the tool used (Database Migration Service, or a manual dump/restore approach), how you validated data completeness/correctness post-migration, and how you handled the cutover (a maintenance window, or a replication-based approach for minimal downtime) - concrete detail on validation and cutover strategy is what shows real migration experience versus a one-line claim.
How do you identify long-running SQL que: Query PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_activity` view filtered for queries running longer than a threshold, or use `pg_stat_statements` (an extension tracking cumulative execution statistics per query) to find queries with the highest total or average execution time across many runs, not just a single slow instance - the extension-based approach is better for finding systemic slow-query patterns rather than just catching one query in the act.
How do you optimize slow-running SQL que: Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the slow query first to see the actual execution plan and where time is really being spent (a sequential scan on a large table where an index scan should be possible is the most common finding), add an index on the columns used in WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY clauses if missing, and check for other common issues (an implicit type cast preventing index use, an overly broad SELECT *, or a query structure forcing the planner into a suboptimal plan) - always re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE after a change to confirm the fix actually improved the plan rather than assuming it did.
You mentioned Terraform and Ansible. Hav: Answer honestly with actual scope and depth - whether you've written playbooks/roles from scratch or primarily run existing ones, and one concrete example (what it automated) to substantiate the claim.
What was the purpose of using Ansible, s: Name the actual use case - OS patching/updates across a fleet of VMs, configuration management (ensuring consistent package versions/config files across servers), application deployment orchestration, or generating compliance/inventory reports - Ansible is typically the tool for configuration-layer automation once Terraform has already provisioned the infrastructure itself.
Which Ansible modules have you used, suc: List the ones actually used with brief context - `yum`/`apt` for package management, `systemd`/`service` for service state, `template` (Jinja2-templated config files, generally preferred over `copy` for anything needing variable substitution), `lineinfile` for targeted config file edits, and `command`/`shell` as an escape hatch for anything without a dedicated idempotent module (used sparingly, since they're not idempotent by default and need explicit `changed_when`/`creates` guards).
Can you explain your Ansible playbook, i: A playbook defines an ordered list of tasks executed against hosts defined in an inventory file/dynamic inventory, using variables (from inventory, `vars` files, or `--extra-vars`) for environment-specific values, with handlers as tasks that only run when notified by another task (e.g. restart a service only if its config file actually changed) - execution flows top to bottom, host by host (or in parallel across hosts, sequentially per host by default), stopping on a host if a task fails unless explicitly configured otherwise.
Can you explain the CI/CD process and ho: Development commits trigger CI (build, unit test, security scan) automatically; a successful build deploys to a QA/staging environment for functional/integration testing; Security's gates (SAST, dependency scanning, image scanning) run as automated pipeline stages rather than a separate manual review, ideally; DevOps owns the pipeline and deployment infrastructure itself; and promotion to Production goes through a final approval gate (manual or automated canary) - the goal is that each team's concerns are encoded as automated pipeline stages rather than manual handoffs and email approvals between teams.
When developers commit code, what happen: The commit (or PR) triggers the CI pipeline automatically: checkout, build, unit tests, static analysis/linting, and security scanning run as automated stages - on merge to main, this typically extends to building a versioned artifact/container image and deploying to a staging environment, with production deployment gated behind a separate approval or automated canary step.
Do you perform any scanning after every: Yes, ideally - static code analysis (SonarQube), dependency vulnerability scanning, and secret scanning should all run automatically on every commit/PR as required CI checks, catching issues at the earliest, cheapest point to fix rather than after the code has already been merged or deployed.
Which tool do you use for code scanning,: Name the actual tool used (SonarQube for self-hosted, SonarCloud for the managed SaaS version) and how it's wired into the pipeline (a required CI stage that fails the build if the Quality Gate doesn't pass) - the specific integration detail (blocking vs. informational) matters more than just naming the tool.
What does SonarQube check, including bug: SonarQube's static analysis flags bugs (likely runtime errors), vulnerabilities (security-relevant code patterns), code smells (maintainability issues - not bugs, but bad practice), and code duplication percentage, then evaluates all of these against a configured Quality Gate (a set of pass/fail thresholds, e.g. 'no new critical vulnerabilities, coverage on new code above 80%') that determines whether the analysis as a whole passes or fails.
What happens if SonarQube Quality Gate f: The CI pipeline should be configured to fail/block the build when the Quality Gate fails, preventing the code from progressing further in the pipeline (merge, deploy) until the specific flagged issues are fixed - treating the Quality Gate as an advisory-only check that doesn't actually block anything defeats its purpose, since it becomes easy to ignore under deadline pressure.
After SonarQube, what are the next stage: Once code quality/security gates pass: build the application artifact, containerize it into a Docker image, scan the image itself for vulnerabilities (a separate check from source code scanning - catches vulnerable base images/dependencies baked into the container), push the scanned image to the artifact registry tagged with a unique identifier (commit SHA), then deploy progressively through environments (Dev auto-deploys, QA runs integration tests, Production requires an approval gate or automated canary validation) before being considered fully released.
